Empirical Research Plan –  UI Payroll-Tax Incidence and Labor-Market Outcomes, 1978-1984  

──────────────────────────────────────────────  

1. Identification Strategy  
Method:  Difference-in-Differences (two-way fixed effects) augmented with an event-study (dynamic DID).  
Why appropriate  
•  Multiple changes in statutory UI payroll-tax rates occur at different dates in different states ⇒ quasi-experimental staggered rollout.  
•  Rich panel (state × industry × quarter, 1978-84) allows (i) state-industry fixed effects to soak up permanent differences and (ii) calendar-time fixed effects to absorb common shocks.  
•  Parallel-trends assumption is empirically testable with pre-period leads in the event-study.  
Extension: Use the mechanical “experience-rating” formula that maps recent benefit outlays into future tax rates as an instrument for the *actual* tax rate (2SLS within the same panel). This weakens concerns that legislatures endogenously raise rates in response to unobserved labor-market conditions.  

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable  
τ_sit  = statutory employer UI payroll-tax rate (average across firms) in state s, industry i, quarter t.  
Main treatment indicator  D_sit  = 1{τ_sit  increases by ≥ x basis points for the first time after t−1}.  Once a state-industry cell is “exposed,” it remains treated.  

Control group  
State-industry cells whose tax rate does *not* change in that quarter provide the contemporaneous counterfactual.  

Treatment timing  
Event date 0 = first quarter the new tax schedule takes effect (usually Jan 1 for most states; we code as Q1). Leads: k = −8,…,−1; lags: k = 0,…,+8.  

(RDD not applicable; no sharp cutoff.)  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1.  Parallel trends: In the absence of a tax-rate change, treated and control state-industries would have evolved similarly.  Plausibility: Short 1978-84 window, control for industry*quarter FE to capture aggregate demand shocks, testable with pre-trends.  
A2.  No anticipatory effects: Firms/workers do not adjust outcomes before the law is enacted.  Plausibility: UI tax changes are typically announced late in the previous year and are small; we check by plotting k = −4,…,−1 coefficients.  
A3.  Stable composition: State-industry cell boundaries (NAICS/SIC definitions) and reporting rules do not change materially.  Plausibility: verified using BLS concordances.  
A4.  SUTVA: A tax hike in state s does not directly affect wages in another state except through general equilibrium (absorbed by time FE).  

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
T1.  Endogenous policy response: States could raise UI taxes when their labor market weakens (reverse causality).  
 •  Include state-specific linear trends and macro controls (state GDP growth).  
 •  2SLS robustness: instrument τ_sit with mechanically predicted rate from the experience-rating formula using lagged benefit payments.  
T2.  Differential recession timing (1980, 1982 recessions) hitting Rust-belt states where taxes also rose.  
 •  Industry*quarter FE capture nation-wide industry cycles; state*quarter macro controls.  
 •  Event-study allows visual inspection – if pre-trends still diverge, drop those events or re-weight.  
T3.  Spillovers / migration of firms across state borders.  
 •  Cluster SEs at the state level to account for spatial correlation.  
 •  Test for border-county employment shifts (placebo outcome).  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast manipulation
library(fixest)       # TWFE + event study
library(ivreg)        # 2SLS if desired
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load & prep -----------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("ui_admin_1978_1984.csv")   # one row: state-industry-quarter

# Basic vars
dt[, post_event  := 0L]
setorder(dt, state, industry, year, quarter)

# Identify first tax hike ≥ 0.1 ppts (example threshold)
dt[, d_tax  := 100*(uip_tax - shift(uip_tax)), by = .(state, industry)]
dt[, event_q := ifelse(d_tax >= 0.10 & shift(cumsum(d_tax >= 0.10), fill = 0)==0,
                       0L, NA_integer_), 
   by = .(state, industry)]
# Fill event time
dt[, event_time := (seq_len(.N) - which(!is.na(event_q))[1]),
   by = .(state, industry)]
dt[, treat := (event_time >= 0)]
dt[, leads_lags := fifelse(abs(event_time) <= 8, event_time, NA_integer_)]

# 2. Main TWFE regression --------------------------------------------------
fe_spec <- feols(wage ~ i(leads_lags, treat, ref = -1) | 
                   state+industry*quarter, 
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state)

summary(fe_spec)

# 3. 2SLS robustness -------------------------------------------------------
# mechanical predicted tax based on lagged benefits
dt[, pred_tax := 0.06 + 0.25*lag(benefit_outlays, 4), by = state] # example formula

iv_spec <- feols(wage ~ treat | state+industry*quarter | pred_tax ~ uip_tax, 
                 data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(iv_spec)

# 4. Additional outcomes ---------------------------------------------------
outcomes <- c("employment", "claims", "denials")
lapply(outcomes, function(y){
    feols(as.formula(paste0(y, " ~ i(leads_lags, treat, ref=-1) | ",
                            "state+industry*quarter")), 
          data = dt, cluster = ~state)
})

# 5. Pre-trend robustness --------------------------------------------------
pretrend_spec <- feols(wage ~ i(leads_lags, treat, ref = -2, collapse = -8:-2) |
                         state+industry*quarter, 
                       data = dt, cluster = ~state)
summary(pretrend_spec)
```

6. Expected Results  
Theory: A payroll tax levied on employers in a competitive labor market is borne largely by workers if labor supply is relatively inelastic.  
•  Wages: decline by ~50–80 % of the statutory tax change within two years (e.g., a 0.5 ppt tax rise → 0.25–0.4 ppt lower wage growth).  
•  Employment: small negative effect, perhaps −0.1 % to −0.3 % (elasticity ≈ −0.05 to −0.10).  
•  Claims: may *decline* because higher costs give firms incentive to contest separations.  
•  Denials: likely to *increase* modestly (moral-hazard mitigation).  

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)  
C1: No differential pre-trends………………1  
C2: No anticipation……………………………1  
C3: Stable composition………………………1  
C4: No spillovers (SUTVA)…………………0  
C5: Treatment exogeneity…………………0  

Total = 3 / 5 – credible but relies on careful robustness and an IV supplement.
